# Judge v2 program — every change paired with a bias metric and an accuracy metric (2026-09-09/10)

Goal (author's instruction 2026-09-09): improve the judge in every way possible, and make sure each
change actually mitigates the bias it targets and improves the judge. Rule of this document: a
change is adopted only if (a) its targeted bias metric moves in the right direction on a paired
test, (b) key-decidable accuracy does not fall, and (c) the final assembled judge (STACK) beats
the current production judge end-to-end on the board metrics. Everything below is registered
before its first call; outcomes are appended under each item.

## Bias catalogue, evidence, mitigation, test

| # | bias | measured on the production judge (Mistral-Large-3, v1 prompt) | mitigation | paired test | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B1 | verbosity / elaboration-as-evidence | beta_len +0.39/1k chars (top cluster +1.32/1k); causal: truncating the correct answer's reasoning drops the correct-verdict rate 0.766 → 0.259 (L1); "ignore length" clause not followed (99.4% prefer the longer of a stub pair) | give the judge something to VERIFY against (reference); remove the both-correct depth criteria (v2 prompt) | J2/J2-R (done: +7.6pp), J3-R (running), **L1-V** (new), F7 confidence gate (done) | partly done |
| B2 | position | second-shown wins 55.1% of single-order votes; flips 9.7–12.8% | dual order + tie-on-flip (in place; J5 showed aggregation is not better) | flip rate and second-shown rate re-measured under v2 and under the reference (free, from the new caches) | free |

Free result recorded 2026-09-09 23:55 (J2-R cache, 944 decidable): when Mistral's and the
reasoning model's independent answers AGREE (63%), the reference is 92% correct and adds +8.1pp
(0.812 → 0.892); when they DISAGREE (37%), the reasoning reference is still 77% correct and adds
+6.9pp (0.705 → 0.774). Showing the reference only on agreement would score 0.823 < 0.849.
Consequence: never gate the reference away; improve the disagree stratum instead (J2-D).

## New registered tests

### L1-V — does the reference remove the elaboration vulnerability? (~2.2k Mistral calls)
L1's 359 top-cluster matches (correct answer longer by ≥ 300 chars), same three arms (original,
truncate, pad), same session, Mistral, v1 prompt, but the question carries the reasoning
reference exactly as in J2-R. Harness: `causal_length.py --reference grok-reasoning`, cache
experiment_results/causal_length/mistral_refgrok.db.
REGISTERED PRIMARY: the truncation drop with the reference is less than HALF of L1's (−0.507),
i.e. drop ≤ 0.25, AND the truncate-arm correct-verdict rate ≥ 0.55 (L1: 0.259). SECONDARY: pad
arm within ±0.03 of original (no padding effect appears). Prediction: drop ≈ 0.15–0.25, truncate
arm ≈ 0.60 — the judge can verify a terse correct answer once it has a reference, which is the
mechanism claim behind B1's mitigation.

### J2-D — two references on the disagree stratum (~1.4k Mistral calls)
Questions where Mistral's S1 answer ≠ the reasoning model's S1 answer (37% of the R3 sample).
Arm: both answers shown as "[Two independent reference solutions — they disagree; at most one is
right]" (order fixed: reasoning model's first), v1 prompt, Mistral, dual order. Comparator: J2-R's
cached verdicts on the same matches (reasoning reference only). Harness `tools/analysis/j2d_two_refs.py`.
REGISTERED: key-decidable accuracy on the disagree stratum vs J2-R's 0.774, paired McNemar
p < 0.05, either direction reported. Prediction: NULL or slightly negative (a second, 12%-correct
candidate is noise); the point is to close the design branch with data.

### FORMAT — style perturbation (CALM-style; ~1.2k Mistral calls; conditional)
Eligibility: key-decidable R3 pairs whose two traces differ in formatting (markdown/LaTeX/list
markers present in one, absent in the other) — prevalence measured before launch and recorded
below; the test runs only if ≥ 150 such pairs exist. PREVALENCE (recorded 2026-09-09 23:55, before
launch, markdown-only definition): 383 of 946 key-decidable R3 pairs have exactly one formatted trace;
the formatted side is the correct one in 270 (70%). Formatting is confounded with model tier (iask 85%,
gpt-4o 78%, arx 63% of traces formatted; the small open models ≤ 9%), which is why only the causal
perturbation can answer the question. Arm: strip the formatting from the formatted
trace (markers removed, content and answer line intact); compare against the cached v1 verdict.
REGISTERED: verdict flip rate toward the unformatted side and the change in correct-verdict rate;
a format bias exists iff correct-verdict rate changes by > 3pp with p < 0.05. Prediction: no
effect (the L1 pad arm already showed bytes without content do nothing).

### STACK — the assembled judge v2, end-to-end (~4k Mistral calls)
Configuration = production template with: the reasoning reference (J2-R) + the v2 mechanics
(J3-R) IF J3-R passes its primary and guards, else v1 mechanics + the ANCHOR rubric of the clean
bareq512_s42 tree instead of the leaf rubric + dual order + confidence kept. Judged on R3's 1,980
matches, Mistral, one session.
REGISTERED (all must hold): (1) all-decidable accuracy ≥ J2-R's 0.849 − 1pp; (2) top-cluster
accuracy ≥ 0.665 − 2pp; (3) top-4 board from the 600 top-cluster matches has ≤ 1 key-order
violation (reasoning judge: 1; Mistral v1: 2); (4) decidable tie rate ≤ 15%; (5) flip rate ≤ J2-R's
12.8%; (6) long-wrong preference on short-correct top-cluster pairs < v1's. Prediction: passes
(1)–(5); (6) improves only if J3-R passes.

- **L1-V (2026-09-10 00:57): PRIMARY FAIL — the reference does NOT remove the elaboration
  vulnerability; it dents it.** 337 matches (of L1's 359; 22 lack a reference) with all three arms:
  original 0.772, truncate 0.350, pad 0.783. Truncation drop 0.421 (142:0, p < 1e-4) against L1's
  0.507 (183:1); the truncate arm rises from 0.259 to 0.350 — one sixth of the gap closed, far from
  the registered halving (drop ≤ 0.25, truncate ≥ 0.55). Secondary PASS: padding does nothing
  (+0.012). Reading: on this subset (top-cluster pairs where the CORRECT answer is the long one) the
  reference adds almost nothing to the original arm (0.772 vs 0.766: the length heuristic already
  picks right here), and when the correct answer is cut to a terse one the judge still follows the
  displayed reasoning of the wrong answer 65% of the time WITH the reference in hand. So the +7.6pp
  of J2-R comes from pairs where the length heuristic points the wrong way, not from disarming the
  heuristic itself. The v1 mechanics never tell the judge to check the final answer before weighing
  the reasoning; v2 does, and J3-R showed +2.2pp exactly where the reference is right. Registered
  follow-up: **L1-V2** below. Cache experiment_results/causal_length/mistral_refgrok.db, output
  l1v_outcome.txt.

### L1-V2 — truncation under the reference AND the v2 mechanics (~2k Mistral calls; registered 2026-09-10 01:00)
L1's matches, three arms, Mistral, reference as in L1-V, SYSTEM template = v2 (prompt_v2.py:
verify the final answer first; a wrong final answer cannot win; no depth criteria). Harness
`causal_length.py --reference grok-reasoning --prompt v2`, cache mistral_refgrok_v2.db.
REGISTERED PRIMARY: truncate-arm correct-verdict rate > L1-V's 0.350 by paired McNemar p < 0.05 on
the common matches (the mechanics, not the reference, are the variable). SECONDARY: original arm
≥ 0.772 − 0.02 (no loss where the long answer is right) and pad within ±0.03 of original.
Prediction: truncate arm 0.45–0.55 — the verify-first instruction moves the judge but does not
cure it; if the truncate arm reaches ≥ 0.55, the v2 mechanics enter STACK as a second arm.

- **J2-D (2026-09-10 01:13): NULL, direction negative — the branch is closed.** Disagree stratum,
  349 key-decidable: two references 0.748 vs the reasoning reference alone 0.774 (−2.6pp, 14:23,
  p = 0.19) vs no reference 0.705. The second candidate dilutes a good reference (reasoning-ref-correct
  stratum, n = 269: 0.862 → 0.810) and rescues only the 42 cases where Mistral's answer was the right
  one (0.571 → 0.690); where neither is right (n = 38) both reference arms sit at 0.368, below the
  no-reference 0.474. Design rule confirmed: ONE reference from the strongest available solver, never a
  set of candidates; when the reference is wrong the judge is worse than with none, so reference
  quality is the whole game (B3). Cache experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/rejudge_mistral_two_refs.db,
  output j2d_outcome.txt.

- **FORMAT (2026-09-10 01:25): no format bias (B5 closed).** 383 key-decidable pairs with exactly one
  markdown-formatted trace, formatting stripped from it: correct-verdict rate 0.786 vs 0.791 original
  (−0.5pp; 6:8; p = 0.79); zero flips toward the unformatted side. Markdown carries no verdict weight

  Cache experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/rejudge_mistral_format_stripped.db, output format_outcome.txt.

- **L1-V2 (2026-09-10 01:58): PRIMARY PASS — the first causal evidence that a prompt change moves
  the elaboration bias; secondary misses by 0.001.** Same 337 matches as L1-V, 0 errors. Truncate arm
  0.433 vs L1-V's 0.350 (+8.3pp; 42:14; p = 0.0002): with the verify-first mechanics the judge keeps the
  terse correct answer 43% of the time instead of 35% (L1 without reference: 26%). Cost: original arm

  experiment_results/causal_length/mistral_refgrok_v2.db, output l1v2_outcome.txt.

### STACK-v2 — the assembled judge with the v2 mechanics (~4k Mistral calls; registered 2026-09-10 02:15)
STACK's configuration with the SYSTEM template = v2 (prompt_v2.v2_system_template on the anchor
rubric); same 1,980 matches, Mistral, one session. Motivation: J3-R (+1.4 overall, +1.1 top cluster,
n.s.) and L1-V2 (+8.3pp on the truncated arm, p = 0.0002; long-wrong preference 0.241). REGISTERED:
the six STACK checks, with (3) evaluated on the ungated board; PRIMARY = check (3) ≤ 1 violation AND
(1)–(2) hold. Prediction: (1),(2),(4),(5),(6) pass; (3) 50/50 — the iask/gemini gap is a 1.7pp key
gap and the v2 long-wrong preference (0.241) may or may not be enough to flip it.

- **RUBRIC-512-R (2026-09-10 02:20): exactly zero for the reasoning judge — B4 closed for both
  tiers, as predicted.** grok-4-1-fast-reasoning, both arms fresh in one session, 3,956 jobs, 0
  errors, 946 key-decidable: cell 0.842 vs generic 0.842 (24:24, p = 1.0); top cluster 0.665 vs 0.665
  (12:12); discursive +0.4 (18:16), quantitative −0.5 (6:8); no anchor beyond ±7pp on n ≤ 144 (all on
  ≤ 4 discordant pairs). Secondary (gain > Mistral's +1.8) fails. Four clean measurements now agree:
  induced cell rubrics are worth 0 to +1pp to any judge tier on keyed questions; the reasoning judge
  reads the answer, not the rubric. Rubric induction is a construction-side cost that buys nothing in
  judging; the anchor rubric is the production choice. Caches
  experiment_results/rubric_512/grok_reasoning_{cell,generic}.db, output grok_reasoning_outcome.txt.

### RK-1 — the verification kit (registered 2026-09-10 03:20, before any judged call; design in docs/rubric_v2_design.md)
Kit per leaf of bareq512_s42 (train-side only): K2 knowledge card (≤ 12 checkable facts/formulas from
≤ 40 solved train items) + K1 failure catalogue (5–8 error patterns with sign and check, from ≤ 20
key-labelled wrong train-side answers of frontier contestants) + K3 two worked neighbours (nearest
train questions of the same leaf by cosine on the 512-slice, option-overlap filtered; built 03:15 for
1,376 of the R3 questions, median top-1 cosine 0.67). Judging: STACK-v2 (reference + v2 mechanics +
anchor rubric) vs STACK-v2 + kit, both fresh and interleaved, Mistral, R3's 1,980 matches (~8k calls).
PRIMARY: kit > STACK-v2 by ≥ +1pp at paired McNemar p < 0.05; SECONDARY: quantitative anchors' gain >
discursive; leakage audit clean (5-grams vs correct options). Prediction: +1 to +3pp, quantitative-led.
Pilot card/catalogue (Chemistry thermodynamics leaf) recorded in the harness log: the card is a list of
formulas with validity conditions, the catalogue is error / sign / check triples — the intended shape.

J6 CAVEAT (recorded 2026-09-10 03:42, after induction and before any judged result): inspection of the
induced texts shows the ladder pipeline's third stage (`synthesizeFinalJudge`, "a short bullet-point
checklist … do NOT include …") compresses the contrastive material into a near-generic checklist again
(the Physics contrastive rubric reads "unit/dimensional consistency (CRITICAL) … force/torque balances
complete (CRITICAL)"; the failure modes survive as one line, "penalizes misconceptions: sign errors,
frame confusion"). So J6 tests authorship and contrastive CORPUS under the existing pipeline, not
contrastive CONTENT delivered to the judge: a null is evidence that the pipeline launders content, not
that failure catalogues are worthless. RK-1 (the kit) bypasses the pipeline and hands the catalogue and
card to the judge verbatim; it is the cleaner test of the idea.

  right and one wrong, i.e. a coin toss the TIE rule correctly refuses to call. STACK-v2's 13.9%

## Deployment rule
The production judge changes only after STACK passes, and the change ships with the measured
before/after table for B1–B8. Cost model of the adopted design: one reasoning call per question
(amortised over every match on it) + two cheap judge calls per match.

## Registered 2026-09-13 (before any call) — POINTWISE: the thesis's founding hypothesis, finally tested directly
The project was built on the bet that an LLM judge is more reliable comparing TWO answers than grading ONE with
little reference. Ninety-plus registered tests measure pairwise judges against the key or against each other;
none has ever run a pointwise arm. This test runs it, changing exactly one variable.
DESIGN. Same judge (grok-4-1-fast-non-reasoning, the JUDGE-SWAP choice), same reasoning reference, same clean
anchor rubric, same verify-first mechanics, same R3 matches — only the FORMAT differs. The pointwise arm grades
each of the 3,689 distinct (question, model) answers ONCE on 0-100 (a fine scale deliberately, so grade
collisions do not handicap the arm) with a confidence; a pair's verdict is then the higher grade, equal grades
being a TIE. Comparator: the already-cached RECIPE-GROK pairwise verdicts on exactly these 1,980 matches
(stack_v2_promptv2_grok.db, all-decidable 0.864). 3,689 calls, no reasoning calls (references are cached).
REGISTERED. (1) PRIMARY, two-sided and stated so the thesis can lose: on the 944 key-decidable pairs, pairwise
accuracy > pointwise accuracy at paired McNemar p < 0.05 SUPPORTS the founding hypothesis; pointwise >= pairwise
REFUTES it, and that is then the honest headline. (2) BOARD: 12-model Spearman rho vs key accuracy from the
grade-derived verdicts, against the pairwise board's rho on the same matches. (3) TIES: the pointwise decidable
tie rate against the pairwise 7.0%. (4) COST: calls per match at the observed question reuse, both formats.
DESCRIPTIVE: the grade distribution and how many distinct values the judge actually uses; AUC of grade against
key correctness (is a grade an informative scalar at all?); whether pointwise does relatively better on the top
cluster, where pairwise is known to be weakest.
PREDICTIONS (on record): pointwise loses on pairs but not by much, 0.82-0.86 against 0.864; boards within 0.02
of each other; pointwise ties higher, 10-20%, because grades collide; pointwise wins on cost, 1.86 calls per
match against 2.00 here and better at higher question reuse. Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/
pointwise_outcome.txt; cache pointwise_grok.db; script tools/analysis/pointwise_judge.py.
  AMENDMENT 2026-09-13, after a 20-call stratified probe and BEFORE any scored run. The probe graded 5 answers
  in each cell of {strong, weak} x {key-correct, key-wrong}: grades were 100,100,100,100,100 / 0,100,0,0,0 /
  100,100,100,100,100 / 0,0,0,0,0. The judge uses the 0-100 scale as a BINARY, 100 when the final answer matches
  the reference and 0 when it does not, in 19 of 20 cases, despite the prompt explicitly forbidding anchoring.
  Two consequences, both recorded before any outcome is known.
  (a) FINDING IN ITS OWN RIGHT: with verify-first mechanics and a reference, pointwise "grading" is not grading.
      It is a verification decision wearing a numeric scale. The registered DESCRIPTIVE readout on how many
      distinct grades the judge uses is therefore promoted to a primary reported result.
  (b) THE ARM AS DESIGNED ANSWERS THE NARROWER QUESTION. Holding the reference constant is the right way to
      isolate FORMAT, but the thesis's actual bet was about grading "without much reference". So the run becomes
      a 2x2 over {pairwise, pointwise} x {reference, no reference}. Two cells are already cached and cost
      nothing: pairwise+reference = RECIPE-GROK (0.864), pairwise-no-reference = the J1 grok cell-rubric arm
      (rejudge_grok.db, 0.743). Two new arms of 3,689 calls each: pointwise+reference, pointwise-no-reference
      (same rubric and mechanics, the reference block simply absent). 7,378 calls total, no reasoning calls.
  REVISED PREDICTIONS, replacing the pre-probe ones, which the probe has already falsified in mechanism:
  pointwise+reference scores HIGH on key-decidable pairs, 0.85-0.90, at or above pairwise's 0.864, because a
  binary verification is exactly what a one-right-one-wrong pair requires, with near-zero ties there and very
  high ties on non-decidable pairs; pointwise-no-reference falls to 0.65-0.78 against pairwise-no-reference's
  0.743; and the 2x2 shows the REFERENCE explaining far more variance than the FORMAT. If that holds, the
  founding hypothesis is not so much refuted as reframed: what the pairwise setup bought was never the
  comparison, it was a place to put verification.

- **POINTWISE arm A (2026-09-13): the founding hypothesis is SUPPORTED on pairs and OVERTURNED on the board.**
  3,674 of 3,689 answers graded (4 content-filter refusals, 11 skips), 941 key-decidable pairs compared against
  the cached pairwise verdicts on exactly those matches. Same judge, reference, rubric, mechanics; only the
  format differs.
  (1) PRIMARY: pairwise 0.864 vs pointwise 0.808, -5.6pp, discordant 87:34, McNemar p = 1.6e-06 -> the thesis's
      founding bet HOLDS for deciding an individual comparison, and holds more strongly on the top cluster
      (0.721 vs 0.649, -7.2pp).
  (2) BOARD, and this is the reversal: the 12-model Spearman rho against key accuracy is 0.9930 from the
      POINTWISE grades and 0.9790 from the pairwise verdicts, on the same 1,971 matches; the raw mean grade,
      with no Bradley-Terry fit at all, gives 0.9860. Both pointwise aggregations beat the pairwise board.
      On the 598 top-cluster matches both formats judged, the top-4 order is
        pairwise   gemini > iask > arx > gpt-4o   (1 key-order violation)
        pointwise  gemini > arx > iask > gpt-4o   (0 violations, exactly the key order)
      That single inversion is the SAME one that appears in ARENA-V2 (iask over gemini by 0.018 logits), in
      ARENA-V2-X20 (4 top-6 violations) and as the broken bridge in GEN-ARENA. Pointwise grading resolves it.
  (3) TIES pointwise 9.4% vs pairwise 7.0%. (4) COST 1.86 calls per match vs 2.00 at this schedule's 2.68x
      question reuse, and the gap widens with reuse because a grade is computed once and reused in every pair
      that answer appears in.
  DESCRIPTIVE: 25 distinct grades used, but 75% of them are 0 or 100 (1,486 and 1,263) - the collapse the probe
  predicted, with a real 25% tail. Grade AUC against key correctness 0.873, mean 84.8 for correct answers and
  19.1 for wrong ones.
  INTERPRETATION. Pairwise is better at DECIDING one comparison; pointwise is better at PRODUCING a ranking.
  The mechanism is visible in the numbers: pairwise errors are systematically correlated - it inverts the same
  frontier near-tie every time, in every board this project has built - while pointwise errors are noisier per
  pair but unbiased across models, so they average out under aggregation. A leaderboard is an aggregate, which
  is why the format that loses 5.6pp per pair wins on rho and on the top-4 order. The honest recommendation is a
  HYBRID: grade pointwise to rank, and spend pairwise calls only where the grades are close, which is exactly
  the frontier where per-pair accuracy matters and where a router reads its argmax.
  Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/pointwise_outcome.txt; script tools/analysis/pointwise_judge.py.
  Arm B (no reference, the 2x2's fourth cell) is running.

## Registered 2026-09-13 (before running, ZERO calls) — HYBRID: grade to rank, compare only where grades are close
POINTWISE arm A showed pairwise winning per pair (0.864 vs 0.808) and pointwise winning the board (rho 0.9930 vs
0.9790, top-4 exact). Both formats have already judged the same 1,980 matches, so every routing rule between
them can be simulated on the cached verdicts at no cost. RULE: for a match, if |grade_a - grade_b| > tau take the
POINTWISE verdict, else take the PAIRWISE one; tau = 0 sends only exact grade ties to the pairwise judge, tau =
100 sends everything. Sweep tau over 0, 1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 60, 100.
REGISTERED READOUT: for each tau, the key-decidable accuracy, the 12-model board rho against key accuracy, the
top-4 key-order violations, and the PAIRWISE BUDGET (fraction of matches routed to the pairwise judge, which
sets the call cost as 1 + 2 x budget calls per match once grades are amortised). tau* = the smallest pairwise
budget that simultaneously reaches accuracy >= pairwise's 0.864 AND top-4 violations = 0. If no tau does both,
report the frontier and say so. PREDICTION: tau* near 10-20, accuracy ~0.87, 0 violations, pairwise budget
25-40%, i.e. roughly half the calls of the all-pairwise arena for a better board. Output
experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/hybrid_outcome.txt; script tools/analysis/hybrid_judge.py.

- **HYBRID (2026-09-13, zero calls): REGISTERED FAIL on two of three clauses, and it dominates pure pairwise.**
  Routing each of the 1,971 doubly-judged matches by grade gap (pointwise when |grade_a - grade_b| > tau,
  pairwise otherwise):

    tau   pairwise%   accuracy   board rho   top-4 viol   calls/match
      0      36.1%      0.874      0.9790         1          2.58
      5      41.3%      0.874      0.9860         1          2.68
     15      45.0%      0.880      0.9790         1          2.76
     30      49.1%      0.883      0.9790         1          2.84
     60      62.0%      0.876      0.9860         1          3.10
    100     100.0%      0.864      0.9790         1          3.86
    (all-pairwise 0.864 / 0.9790 / 1 / 2.00; all-pointwise 0.808 / 0.9930 / 0 / 1.86)

  WHAT PASSED: per-pair accuracy peaks at 0.883 at tau = 30, ABOVE both parents (+1.9pp on pairwise, +7.5pp on
  pointwise). Mixing the formats genuinely decides individual comparisons better than either alone.
  WHAT FAILED, against my registered prediction of tau* near 10-20 with 0 violations at 25-40% budget and
  roughly half the calls: (a) NO tau reaches 0 top-4 violations. The inversion returns as soon as any pairwise
  verdict enters, even at tau = 0, because the close-grade pairs ARE the frontier pairs and the frontier is
  exactly where pairwise errs. Pointwise's clean top-4 is fragile, not additive. (b) The hybrid is never
  CHEAPER: cost is 1.86 + 2 x budget, and the smallest budget available is already 36% because that many pairs
  carry exactly equal grades (a consequence of the 0/100 collapse - those are the both-right and both-wrong
  pairs). To undercut pure pairwise you would need a budget below 7%, which this grade distribution cannot give.
  CONCLUSION, and it is the useful one: PURE PAIRWISE IS DOMINATED. It is beaten on per-pair accuracy by the
  hybrid (0.883 vs 0.864), beaten on the board by pointwise (0.9930 vs 0.9790, 0 violations vs 1), and beaten on
  cost by pointwise (1.86 vs 2.00 calls per match). The real choice is between POINTWISE when the product is a
  ranking - cheapest, best correlated, correct at the top - and the HYBRID when the product is an individual
  verdict, at 2.84 calls per match. A router, which reads an argmax off a ranking, should use pointwise.
  Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/hybrid_outcome.txt; script tools/analysis/hybrid_judge.py.

- **POINTWISE arm B and the completed 2x2 (2026-09-13).** 3,669 answers graded with NO reference (4 refusals),
  940 key-decidable pairs against the cached no-reference pairwise arm (J1's grok cell-rubric verdicts).

      key-decidable accuracy      pairwise    pointwise    format effect
      with a reference              0.864       0.808          +5.6pp
      no reference                  0.746       0.678          +6.8pp
      reference effect             +11.8pp     +13.0pp

      12-model board rho          pairwise    pointwise
      with a reference             0.9790      0.9930   (top-4: 1 violation vs 0)
      no reference                 0.9650      0.9860

  THE 2x2 SETTLES THE FOUNDING QUESTION. (i) The FORMAT effect is real, consistent and modest: comparing beats
  grading by 5.6 to 6.8pp per pair, in both reference conditions, so the thesis's bet is confirmed and it
  replicates. (ii) The REFERENCE effect is about TWICE the format effect: 11.8pp for pairwise and 13.0pp for
  pointwise. What the framework gained most from was not the comparison, it was having somewhere to put
  verification. (iii) The board reversal replicates in BOTH cells: pointwise correlates better with the key than
  pairwise whether or not a reference is present (0.9930 vs 0.9790, and 0.9860 vs 0.9650). (iv) Without a
  reference everything degrades and abstention doubles: pointwise ties 20.5% (from 9.4%), pairwise 16.1%
  (from 7.0%).
  Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/pointwise_noref_outcome.txt.

## Registered 2026-09-13 (before running, ZERO calls) — SCHED: this framework's match-making vs Varco Arena's tournament
Varco Arena (arXiv:2411.01281) ranks models by a single-elimination tournament per prompt, (n-1) matches per
prompt, and names as its own limitation that "rooms for improvement exist for more informative match-making
algorithm". This framework has one: a Bradley-Terry racing scheduler that stratifies by taxonomy cell, budgets
per (cell, pair) and caps query reuse. Compare them at MATCHED BUDGET in the synthetic arena, so no judge calls.
SETUP. Universe: the 2,812 x12 questions x 12 models with known key correctness; ground truth = each model's key
accuracy. Judge = the LEAF-POWER noise model: on key-decidable pairs the correct winner with probability 1-p, on
non-decidable pairs a random winner with probability 0.8 and otherwise a tie. p swept over 0.10, 0.228 (Mistral's
measured rate) and 0.40, echoing Varco's own sweep of judge accuracy. 20 seeds per configuration.
ARMS, all at the SAME 9,144-match budget as the real campaign: (a) THIS FRAMEWORK — the actual x12 MAIN schedule
replayed triple for triple, so it is the real scheduler's output and not a reimplementation; (b) SINGLE
ELIMINATION — random bracket per question, 11 matches per question, on 831 questions to match the budget;
(c) RANDOM PAIRING — 9,144 uniform (question, pair) draws; (d) ROUND ROBIN — 138 questions x all 66 pairs.
REGISTERED READOUT: (1) GLOBAL board Spearman rho against key accuracy and top-4 key-order violations, per arm
per noise level; (2) PER-ANCHOR quality, the mean rho over the 14 depth-1 anchors, which is what the cell
stratification was actually designed to buy and what a router consumes. PREDICTION: single elimination edges
this framework's schedule on the GLOBAL board, by under 0.02 rho, because the bracket spreads comparisons across
the whole roster while the cell design concentrates them inside cells; this framework wins the PER-ANCHOR
readout decisively, because the tournament never guarantees coverage within a cell; random pairing tracks single
elimination globally and loses per anchor; round robin is best globally at equal budget but covers only 138
questions, so it is the worst per anchor. If single elimination also wins per anchor, the cell-stratified design
has no scheduling justification and that must be said plainly. Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/
sched_outcome.txt; script tools/analysis/sched_compare.py.

- **SCHED (2026-09-13, zero calls): the tournament does NOT beat this framework's scheduler, and loses badly at
  the top of the board.** 12 models, 2,778 questions, budget 9,063 matches, 20 seeds per cell, judge noise swept.

      flip 0.100        global rho        top-4 viol     per-anchor rho
      THIS FRAMEWORK   0.9881 +-0.0060    0.05 +-0.22    0.9092 +-0.0120
      SINGLE ELIM      0.9907 +-0.0063    0.65 +-0.67    0.8845 +-0.0196
      RANDOM PAIRS     0.9906 +-0.0061    0.70 +-0.73    0.9007 +-0.0125
      flip 0.228 (Mistral's measured rate)
      THIS FRAMEWORK   0.9832 +-0.0097    0.15 +-0.37    0.8346 +-0.0229
      SINGLE ELIM      0.9809 +-0.0146    1.40 +-1.05    0.8018 +-0.0312
      RANDOM PAIRS     0.9843 +-0.0134    0.85 +-0.99    0.8213 +-0.0180
      flip 0.400
      THIS FRAMEWORK   0.9154 +-0.0476    0.65 +-0.67    0.4949 +-0.0709
      SINGLE ELIM      0.8935 +-0.0396    2.60 +-1.31    0.4685 +-0.0661
      RANDOM PAIRS     0.9013 +-0.0568    1.90 +-1.41    0.4884 +-0.0579

  (1) GLOBAL BOARD: the four arms are indistinguishable at realistic noise, every gap inside one standard
      deviation; at flip 0.40 this framework is ahead (0.9154 vs 0.8935). My prediction that single elimination
      would edge it globally is right only at the lowest noise and by 0.0026, which is noise, and it reverses as
      the judge degrades.
  (2) TOP-4 VIOLATIONS, the frontier a router actually reads: this framework wins at every noise level by a wide
      margin - 0.05 vs 0.65, 0.15 vs 1.40, 0.65 vs 2.60, i.e. four to thirteen times fewer inversions. The
      mechanism is the racing rule: it keeps spending on pairs whose order is still undecided, which are the top
      pairs, whereas a bracket lets the strongest models meet at most once per prompt and often not at all.
  (3) PER-ANCHOR: this framework > single elimination at every noise, by 0.02 to 0.03 rho. Real, but "decisive"
      as predicted overstates it.
  DISCLOSURE OF A FLAW IN MY OWN READOUT: the ROUND ROBIN row's per-anchor column is not comparable and must not
  be quoted. At matched budget round robin covers only 137 questions, about 10 per anchor, so 0 of 14 anchors
  clear the readout's own filter of >= 100 matches and >= 20 questions; the figure printed is computed from the
  stray anchor that qualifies in a few seeds. This framework and single elimination both qualify 14 of 14.
  POSITIONING AGAINST VARCO ARENA: their tournament is a budget-efficiency result against reference-ANCHORED
  comparison, and it is not a match-making result against an adaptive scheduler. Their own stated limitation,
  "rooms for improvement exist for more informative match-making algorithm", is what this framework supplies,
  and the measured benefit is concentrated exactly where their bracket is weakest, at the top of the ranking.
  Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/sched_outcome.txt; script tools/analysis/sched_compare.py.

## Registered 2026-09-13 (before running, ZERO calls) — FRONTIER: is the top-cluster inversion dilution, judge capability, or the dataset?
Every top-cluster readout in this project restricts by MODEL PAIR and then fits the board on ALL of that pair's
matches, including the both-right and both-wrong ones, where the key carries no signal and FLIP-PROV measured a
21.7% flip rate. So three explanations have never been separated: (a) DILUTION, the signal-free pairs swamping
the discriminative ones; (b) JUDGE CAPABILITY, the judge genuinely cannot tell the frontier models apart;
(c) DATASET, the reserved split leaving too few questions on which the frontier models actually differ.
TESTS, all on cached verdicts. (A) DATASET: for each of the 6 top-4 pairs, on the pool of record and on the R3
sample, the number of questions where the two models DIFFER by the key, the win split, the implied win rate with
its binomial SE, and whether the key's own accuracy gap between them is resolvable at that n. (B) DILUTION:
refit the top-4 board on DECIDABLE matches only, separately for the pairwise (RECIPE-GROK) and pointwise arms,
and compare violations against the all-matches board (pairwise 1, pointwise 0).
REGISTERED READOUT: if the decidable-only pairwise board reaches 0 violations, the inversion was DILUTION and
the judge is fine; if it stays inverted while the pointwise one is clean, it is CAPABILITY specific to the
pairwise format; if the key's own arx/iask gap is not resolvable at the available n, it is the DATASET and no
judge of any kind could settle that pair. PREDICTION: mixed - dilution explains part of it, and the arx-iask gap
(key 0.834 vs 0.817, 1.7pp) is at or below the resolution the reserved pool supports.
Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/frontier_outcome.txt; script tools/analysis/frontier_probe.py.

- **FRONTIER (2026-09-13, zero calls): the dataset is exonerated; the inversion is manufactured on the pairs the
  key calls ties, and the arena sample is too thin to settle the rest.**
  (A) DATASET. All six top-4 pairs are separable by the pool of record. Questions where the two models differ,
  and the stronger model's win rate on them: gemini/arx 398 at 0.837 +-0.019, gemini/iask 475 at 0.842 +-0.017,
  gemini/gpt-4o 680 at 0.904 +-0.011, arx/iask 301 at 0.595 +-0.028, arx/gpt-4o 502 at 0.781 +-0.018,
  iask/gpt-4o 493 at 0.728 +-0.020. Even the closest pair, arx over iask, sits 3.4 SE from chance. The reserved
  split did NOT take away the discriminating evidence: it is there, 301 questions of it, and the key's 1.7pp
  accuracy gap understates a head-to-head signal of 0.595.
  (B) DILUTION alone does not explain it. Refitting the top-4 board on DECIDABLE matches only leaves pairwise
  still inverted (iask over arx, accuracy 0.721 on those), and it BREAKS pointwise (arx over gemini). Caveat
  that limits how hard this can be read: 265 decidable top-4 matches spread over six pairs is about 44 per
  pair, so both decidable-only boards are underpowered.
  (C) MECHANISM, and this is the finding. On the 333 non-decidable top-4 pairs - where the key says the two
  answers are equally correct or equally wrong - PAIRWISE declares a winner 52% of the time, and those invented
  verdicts are sharply asymmetric: iask +34 net wins, arx -44, a 78-point swing between exactly the two models
  whose order is inverted, with 73% of the invented winners going to the LONGER answer. POINTWISE abstains on
  69% of the same pairs, its residual asymmetry is a quarter the size (iask +0, arx -12) and its length
  preference is 55%, near chance. So the pairwise board's inversion is largely built on questions that carry no
  correctness signal at all, by a length-correlated preference - which is L1's elaboration-as-evidence finding
  and FLIP-PROV's 21.7% non-decidable flip rate, now shown to move a specific pair in a specific direction.
  WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT, and it is cheap: stop judging frontier pairs at random and judge the 301 questions on
  which arx and iask actually differ - 602 calls either format. Registered separately if run.
  Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/frontier_outcome.txt; script tools/analysis/frontier_probe.py.

## Registered 2026-09-13 (before any call) — ARXIASK: the clean capability test on the discriminating evidence
FRONTIER showed the arx/iask inversion is built largely on pairs the key calls ties. This removes that channel by
construction: judge ONLY the 301 pool questions on which arx_0314 and iask_pro actually differ, where the key
says arx wins 179 and iask 122 (0.595 +- 0.028). Every match is decidable, so no signal-free pair can contribute.
ARMS, same judge (grok-4-1-fast-non-reasoning), reference, anchor rubric and mechanics as the campaign:
PAIRWISE dual order (602 calls) and POINTWISE grading of both answers (602 calls). 1,204 calls total.
REGISTERED: (1) PRIMARY, per format, the judged win rate for arx over iask, tested against 0.5 by a two-sided
binomial - recovering the true order means a rate above 0.5 at p < 0.05; (2) accuracy against the key on these
301, where chance is 0.5 and the campaign's decidable top-4 accuracy was 0.721 pairwise; (3) does the judged win
rate track the key's 0.595; (4) LENGTH CONTROL - the share of judged verdicts going to the longer answer, and
the same win rate recomputed on the subset where the two traces are within 20% of each other in length.
PREDICTIONS: pairwise accuracy 0.72-0.80 but an arx win rate of 0.45-0.55, i.e. it still fails to recover the
order, and its winners are the longer answer more than 60% of the time (iask averages 1,303 characters against
arx's 860); pointwise accuracy 0.65-0.75 with an arx win rate of 0.52-0.62, recovering the order weakly; the
length-matched subset moves both toward the key. If BOTH formats recover the order here, the inversion is
entirely an artefact of scheduling frontier matches on signal-free questions, which is a clean, actionable
result for the paper. Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/arxiask_outcome.txt; cache arxiask.db;
script tools/analysis/arxiask_probe.py.

- **SCHEDULING (2026-09-13, zero calls): the match scheduler IS the problem, and the fix needs no answer key.**
  Asked whether the frontier fails to resolve because the scheduler picks the wrong matches. It does. Across the
  six top-4 pairs on the pool of record (3,358 questions with extracted answers for all four models):
    * the two candidates give DIFFERENT final answers on only 16.9% of question-pairs;
    * of those disagreeing pairs, 79.6% are key-decidable;
    * of the pairs where the two answers AGREE, 0.04% are key-decidable - essentially none.
  So a scheduler that matches a pair only on questions where their own extracted final answers DISAGREE keeps
  99.8% of every decidable pair in the pool while judging 16.9% of the matches: a six-fold budget reduction that
  simultaneously deletes the channel FRONTIER identified, because the signal-free pairs - the ones on which
  pairwise invents a winner 52% of the time, 73% of them the longer answer, worth +34/-44 between arx and iask -
  are never scheduled at all. The rule uses NO answer key and no judge: it compares the two candidates' own
  extracted answers, which the arena already parses.
  This reframes the campaign's cost result. x12 spent 9,144 matches at a mean of 1.59 per (cell, pair) slot, and
  roughly two thirds of every frontier pair's matches landed on questions that could not discriminate them. The
  same board is reachable with about a sixth of the frontier budget, and cleaner, because the discarded matches
  were not merely uninformative but actively biased.
  CAVEAT to state in the paper: the rule presumes an extractable final answer, so it transfers to multiple
  choice and to verifier-shaped tasks such as MATH, and not to open-ended generation where "the same answer" is
  undefined. On IFEval-shaped tasks the analogous rule is disagreement on the constraint checker's output.
  Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/scheduling_probe.txt.

## Registered 2026-09-13 (before any call) — REGEN: grok-4-1-fast-reasoning as a FAIR arena contestant
The reasoning model has already solved the pool at 0.860, second only to gemini, but under an answer-only JSON
prompt: mean response 361 characters against the contestants' 900-1,500 full chain-of-thought solutions. Given
the length preference measured in FRONTIER (73% of invented winners are the longer answer), entering it on those
traces would penalise it systematically. This regenerates its answers under the CONTESTANTS' prompt shape: the
MMLU-Pro chain-of-thought instruction, options lettered A-J, step-by-step working, ending in "the answer is (X)".
3,445 pool questions, one call each, no judging.
REGISTERED READOUTS, before any downstream use: (1) accuracy on the pool under the CoT prompt against the 0.860
it scored under the answer-only prompt, and the per-question agreement between the two runs - a large gap means
the prompt, not the model, moves the score and both numbers must then be reported; (2) the trace-length
distribution against the 12 contestants', since fairness of entry is exactly what this run is for; (3) the share
of responses from which a final answer can be extracted. ADMISSION RULE fixed now: the model is admitted as a
contestant only if its median trace length falls inside the contestants' range and extraction succeeds on more
than 98% of responses; otherwise it stays a key-level data point and that is reported instead.
PREDICTION: accuracy within 2pp of 0.860, median length 700-1,400 characters, extraction above 99%.
Output experiment_results/judge_solve/regen_grok_reasoning_cot.txt; cache grok-reasoning-cot.db.

- **ARXIASK (2026-09-13): the frontier does not resolve because the REFERENCE fails on exactly the questions
  that discriminate. Neither format recovers the order; the cause is now measured end to end.**
  302 pool questions where arx_0314 and iask_pro differ (key: arx 179, iask 123, rate 0.593), every match
  decidable by construction, 1,196 calls, 2 content-filter refusals.
    format      judged  ties   arx win rate   binomial p   accuracy vs key   winner is longer
    pairwise      299    49       0.496          0.95           0.612              57%
    pointwise     297    42       0.561          0.060          0.667              51%
  (1) NEITHER recovers the key order at p < 0.05. Pointwise is much closer to the truth (0.561 against 0.593)
      and pairwise is at chance (0.496). (4) LENGTH IS NOT THE EXPLANATION HERE: on the 48-51 length-matched
      questions the rates are unchanged (pairwise 0.490, pointwise 0.562), even though iask's traces average
      1,590 characters against arx's 911. The length effect measured in FRONTIER lives on the signal-free pairs,
      not on the discriminating ones.
  (2) THE CAUSE. The reference (grok-4-1-fast-reasoning) scores 0.860 on the pool but only 0.726 on these 299
      discriminating questions - the questions that separate two frontier models are the ones the reference also
      fails. And the judge follows it almost deterministically:
        reference CORRECT (217): pairwise 0.788, pointwise 0.856
        reference WRONG    (82): pairwise 0.146, pointwise 0.160
      Below chance when misled, because the judge actively selects the model agreeing with a wrong reference.
      The arithmetic reproduces the observed totals: 0.726 x ~0.82 + 0.274 x ~0.15 = 0.63.
  THE GENERAL STATEMENT FOR THE THESIS: a reference-free arena's ability to order two models is bounded by the
  reference's accuracy ON THE SUBSET WHERE THOSE MODELS DIFFER, which is systematically far below its headline
  accuracy - here 0.726 against 0.860. Ranking the frontier therefore needs a reference stronger than the models
  being ranked on precisely their hardest questions. With gemini at 0.913 that means a reference above roughly
  0.95 on the hard subset, which no model available to this project reaches. This closes the loop with J1
  (frontier divergence is the judge's capability ceiling), J2-R (the reference is what lifted the judge), REF-SC
  (self-consistency of the same reference model gains nothing) and GEN-ARENA (0.935 where the reference is an
  EXACT verifier). The escape is not a better judge or more matches: it is a task with a checker.
  Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/arxiask_outcome.txt; script tools/analysis/arxiask_probe.py.

- **Two exploratory probes (2026-09-13, zero calls), NOT registered, feeding the next round of tests.**
  PROBE B, can the judge judge what it cannot solve? On the 242 arx/iask discriminating questions the judge
  model itself (grok-4-1-fast-non-reasoning) scores 0.388, against 0.578 on the pool: it fails 61% of the
  questions it is asked to adjudicate. Verdict accuracy splits accordingly - judge solved it: pairwise 0.713,
  pointwise 0.798; judge failed it: 0.554 and 0.575. CONFOUND to resolve before this is quoted: reference
  accuracy on those same subsets is 0.872 and 0.628, so judge ability and reference correctness co-vary with
  question difficulty and this probe cannot separate them. The clean version is a 2x2 conditioning on both.
  PROBE C, is the GROUND TRUTH itself confounded by prompt shape? The eval roster mixes shot counts in the model
  names. One base family spans 0.046 across configurations (claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022 0.779, claude-3.5-sonnet
  0.771, sonnet-3.5_0shots 0.733). That spread is LARGER than the arx/iask frontier gap of 0.017 and comparable
  to gemini/arx 0.079 and iask/gpt-4o 0.067. And gemini-3.1-pro, the top scorer at 0.913, is the only frontier
  entry whose name declares a 5-shot configuration while arx_0314 and iask_pro declare none. If part of gemini's
  lead is a few-shot advantage, then the key ranking that this whole project validates against is itself partly
  a prompting artefact. REGEN gives an independent handle on the size of the effect: the same model scored 0.860
  under an answer-only prompt and is running near 0.814 under the chain-of-thought prompt, a 4.6pp swing from
  prompt shape alone. This is a limitation to measure and disclose, not to explain away.

- **FILTER-BOARD (2026-09-13, zero calls): the answer-disagreement filter is strictly safe on the board.**
  Applying the filter to R3's 1,971 doubly-judged matches keeps 1,264 of them (64.1%; the rate is 16.9% on
  frontier pairs alone and higher here because weak pairs disagree often) and retains ALL 941 key-decidable
  pairs - not 99.8% but 100% on this sample.
    pairwise   all 1,971: rho 0.9790, 1 top-4 violation | filtered 1,264: rho 0.9860, 1 violation
    pointwise  all 1,971: rho 0.9930, 0 violations      | filtered 1,264: rho 0.9930, 0 violations
  Decidable accuracy is identical in both cases (0.864 and 0.808) because no decidable pair is dropped. So the
  filter costs nothing and improves the pairwise board, which validates shipping it as the scheduler option.
- **ABSTAIN (2026-09-13, zero calls): NEGATIVE - confidence-gated abstention does not beat answering.**
  The judge scores ~0.15 when the reference is wrong, so abstaining on likely-wrong references ought to help.
  The reference's own confidence does carry signal on the 242 discriminating questions: it is correct 0.477 in
  the sub-90 bin, 0.718 at 90-99 and 0.896 at 100. But every abstention threshold LOSES against always
  answering: pairwise 0.698 at T=0 against 0.686 (T=90), 0.655 (T=95), 0.576 (T=100); pointwise 0.733 against
  0.700, 0.671, 0.583. Abstention discards the cases the judge would have got right faster than it saves the
  ones it would have got wrong. Third confidence-based mitigation to fail, after gating the reference on solver
  agreement (worse) and showing the confidence to the judge (REF-CONF, null): the confidence signal is real and
  calibrated but never sharp enough to act on.
  Outputs experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/{filterboard_outcome.txt, abstain_outcome.txt}.

## Registered 2026-09-14 (before running, ZERO calls) — PROMPT-AUDIT: is the ground truth itself prompt-confounded?
Probe C found the eval roster mixes prompt configurations in its model names, that one base family spans 0.046
across configurations, and that gemini-3.1-pro - the top scorer and the reference point of every headline - is
the only frontier entry declaring a 5-shot setup while arx_0314 and iask_pro declare none. The key ranking is
the ground truth this entire project validates against, so the size of that confound has to be measured and
disclosed rather than assumed small.

trace length and the rate of missing or unparseable predictions - if declared 0-shot models fail extraction more
often, part of their deficit is formatting rather than capability. (2) WITHIN-FAMILY: accuracy spread for base
models appearing under more than one configuration, stated with the caveat that version and configuration are
partly confounded in those names. (3) CONTROLLED ESTIMATE, the only clean one: REGEN is the same model on the
same questions under two prompts (answer-only 0.860 versus the contestants' chain-of-thought), so report the
PAIRED difference, its standard error and the per-question flip counts on whatever share of the 3,445 has
completed. (4) IMPACT: list the frontier gaps that are SMALLER than the controlled estimate, which are the
orderings the ground truth cannot safely support.
PREDICTION: a prompt effect in the 3-5pp range, which would leave arx/iask (0.017) unsafe, iask/gpt-4o (0.067)
and gemini/arx (0.079) marginal but probably surviving, and everything below the top cluster unaffected.
Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/prompt_audit.txt; script tools/analysis/prompt_audit.py.

- **MATCH FILTER shipped as an option (2026-09-14).** `matchFilter` TOML key, default `"none"` which is the
  historical code path byte for byte (the filter returns the caller's own list instance and a test asserts it),
  and `"answerDisagreement"` which cuts a (cell, pair)'s candidate questions to those where the two models' own
  `eval_results.pred` values differ. Validated at parse time, threaded exactly as maxQueryReuse is, and applied
  at all three question-choice sites; the random scheduler is deliberately left unfiltered since it is the null
  baseline. NO KEY IS READ - the predicate takes two nullable strings and unit tests assert its inputs.
  DEGRADATION, which is why this is an option at all: a missing prediction on either side is UNDETERMINED and
  the question is KEPT; if filtering starves a slot the unfiltered set is used and one line is logged naming the
  cell and pair; if a corpus has no usable predictions the filter declares itself INERT once and behaves as
  "none". A per-run summary line and a validation CSV report candidates before and after, fallbacks and matches.
  GATES: 307 tests green (11 new); stage-0a replay bit-identical with the filter off, the DIFFERS lines being
  the same P7 float drift with the same values; pool re-pinned; frozen triples clean.
  ZERO-CALL DEMONSTRATION (`gradlew matchFilterPlan`, key blanked out of the matrix so a schedule that moved
  would be reading it): on the frontier the filter offers the judge 3,451 of 20,448 question-pairs, 16.9% - the
  SCHEDULING probe's headline reproduced independently from the Kotlin side with no simulation. Run-wide the
  match count falls only from 42,300 to 38,910 (92.0%), for two honest reasons: across a 12-model roster most
  pairs are far apart and already disagree (59.6% of candidates survive), and a pair that never resolves spends
  its whole per-(leaf, pair) budget either way, so on the frontier the benefit is that the same budget buys
  discriminating matches instead of signal-free ones rather than fewer matches. The match counts beyond the
  16.9% line come from a stub judge and are a simulation of the measured decidability structure, stated as such.
  PROVENANCE CORRECTION: the implementation landed in commit 7155bea, whose message is about Probes B and C.
  That is a mistake of mine - I committed while the agent had its files staged, so eight Kotlin and test files
  were swept in under the wrong message. Nothing is lost and the tree is correct; history was not rewritten. The
  feature's commits are 7155bea (implementation) and 0a76596 (plan-only harness).

  headroom MMLU-Pro lost; and the pointwise board advantage does not survive small samples.**
  (3) THE CLEAN 2x2, which retires Probe B's confound. Conditioning verdict accuracy on BOTH whether the judge
  model itself solved the question and whether the reference was right:
        pairwise   judge solved / reference right  n=82  0.780 | judge FAILED / reference right  n=93  0.796
                   judge solved / reference wrong  n=12  0.250 | judge FAILED / reference wrong  n=55  0.145
        pointwise  judge solved / reference right  n=82  0.854 | judge FAILED / reference right  n=92  0.837
                   judge solved / reference wrong  n=12  0.417 | judge FAILED / reference wrong  n=54  0.130
      Holding the reference fixed, the judge's own ability to solve the question makes essentially NO difference
      (0.780 against 0.796 for pairwise; 0.854 against 0.837 for pointwise). Probe B's apparent capability
      effect was entirely the reference confound. This is a positive result for the architecture: a cheap judge
      does not need to be able to answer the question, it needs to be told the right answer.

      is the natural venue for frontier work once MMLU-Pro's 8.8% frontier budget runs out.

      against that anchor's OWN key accuracy (64-274 matches each): pointwise wins 4, pairwise 8, one tie -
      against the global result of 0.9930 to 0.9790 on 1,971 matches. Pointwise verdicts are noisier per pair
      (0.808 against 0.864), so at small n the noise dominates and the unbiasedness only pays once there are
      enough matches to average it out. A FIRST READOUT OF MINE WAS FLAWED AND IS SUPERSEDED: it scored every
      anchor against GLOBAL key accuracy; corrected, the conclusion is unchanged (4-8-1 rather than 3-9-1).
      The pattern in WHICH anchors is not noise: pointwise wins Biology, Chemistry, Engineering and Math and
      ties Physics, while pairwise wins Philosophy, Psychology, Other, Economics, History and Law. Grading wins
      where the answer is checkable and loses where it is discursive - the same axis as RK-1b's data card
      (quantitative +3.0, discursive +0.6) and GEN-ARENA (MATH 0.935 with an exact verifier, IFEval 0.658 with a
      constraint list). UNIFYING RULE for the paper: grade where answers are checkable, compare where they are not.

## Registered 2026-09-14 (before any call) — ARENA-13: a 13th contestant, and self-preference measured on purpose
grok-4-1-fast-reasoning was ADMITTED by REGEN (median trace 886, extraction 99.6%) and sits 2nd on the pool at
0.849, between gemini (0.913) and arx (0.834). Admitting it naively is CIRCULAR: it is also the judge's
reference, and its answer coincides with that reference on 92.7% of pool questions, so it would win by agreeing
with itself. Two arms, sharing their frontier matches so the contrast is paired.
ARM A, PRIMARY, ensemble-referenced. The 12 new pairs only - every existing verdict is reused - at 150 matches
per pair, 1,800 matches, single order, grok-4-1-fast-non-reasoning, v2 mechanics, the routed anchor's rubric.
The REFERENCE is the leave-out majority of the eight strongest contestants EXCLUDING the match's own models;
ENSEMBLE-REF measured that construction at 0.833-0.880, matching the grok reference's 0.860, and it contains no
grok model, so there is no circularity. Candidates are drawn where the two contestants' own answers disagree
(the shipped filter; 85% of such pairs are key-decidable) and where the ensemble has a decisive majority.
ARM B, self-reference. The four frontier pairs (against gemini, arx, iask, gpt-4o), the SAME 600 matches as in
arm A, re-judged with the GROK reference - the self-reference. 600 calls. 2,400 calls in total.
REGISTERED. (1) BOARD: on the 13-model board from arm A, grok-4-1-fast-reasoning places 2nd or 3rd, consistent
with its key rank of 2nd. (2) STABILITY: the 12 existing models keep their ARENA-V2 order, Kendall tau >= 0.90.
(3) NEW-PAIR ACCURACY: key-decidable accuracy on the new pairs >= 0.85, the level ARENA-V2 reached. (4)
SELF-PREFERENCE, the point of arm B: on the shared frontier matches, the judged win rate for the new contestant
is HIGHER with its own reference than with the ensemble reference, tested by paired McNemar. PREDICTIONS: it
places 2nd or 3rd; tau >= 0.95; new-pair accuracy 0.85-0.90 since most new pairs are cross-tier; and the
self-preference effect is +10 to +25pp, which if confirmed is a measured number this literature lacks and a
direct warning against any arena whose judge, reference and contestants share a vendor.
Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/arena13_outcome.txt; cache arena13.db; script tools/analysis/arena13.py.

  (1) FAIL: with the INDEPENDENT ensemble reference the new contestant places FIRST (theta +2.156), above gemini

   endorses - not self-preference. Kitagawa gives composition +0.116 and residual -0.037, and the
   registered cell-matched test gives McNemar p=0.45. The claim is now REFERENCE-AGREEMENT LEAKAGE.]
  (4) CONFIRMED: on the 598 shared frontier matches its win rate is 0.697 under the ensemble reference and

      shared reference is real and large. It is below the +10 to +25pp I predicted, and it is decisive.
  [WITHDRAWN by CONSENSUS-FIT (2026-09-14): fitted, the consensus advantage accounts for 9% of the gap,
   not the whole of it, and the model-level design cannot identify it at all (accuracy and agreement
   correlate 0.982 across the roster, VIF 27.5). POSITION-FULL then attributed 85% of the gap to
   single-order presentation, and PLACEBO-ENTRY (4) closed the question: the residual +0.045 theta has a
   bootstrap CI of [-0.068, +0.186], so the ordering is UNRESOLVED at this budget, not mis-ranked. The
   paragraph below is kept as the record of what was believed on the day, and is not a finding.]
  THE MECHANISM BEHIND (1), measured rather than assumed. How often each model's own answer matches the
  leave-out ensemble reference, against its key accuracy:
      arx_0314        agrees 0.897 | key 0.834          gemini-3.1-pro  agrees 0.865 | key 0.912
      grok-reasoning  agrees 0.882 | key 0.853          gpt-4o          agrees 0.848 | key 0.750
      iask_pro        agrees 0.878 | key 0.811
  Gemini is the MOST accurate model and the LEAST consensus-aligned of the frontier, because a model that is
  better than the field is right precisely where the field is wrong, and so deviates from any majority built
  out of that field. A judge instructed to verify against such a reference rewards resemblance to the consensus,
  not correctness, and the two come apart exactly at the top of the board.
  CONSEQUENCE, and this is the through-line of the judge programme: reference-based judging measures AGREEMENT
  WITH THE REFERENCE, and the gap between that and correctness is widest for the best model in the field. It
  explains ARXIASK (the judge is right 0.79-0.86 when the reference is right and 0.15 when it is wrong), the
  persistent frontier inversions in ARENA-V2 and X20, and why GEN-ARENA reached 0.935 on MATH: an exact verifier
  is the one reference with no consensus bias. Two corollaries for the paper. A stronger reference helps only if
  it is stronger ON THE DISCRIMINATING QUESTIONS. And an ENSEMBLE reference, which looked like the clean fix
  here, carries its own systematic bias against the very model it is meant to rank first.

## Registered 2026-09-14 (before looking at any result, ZERO calls) — DECOMP: is the +7.9pp self-preference, or answer coincidence?
ARENA-13 (4) compared the new contestant's win rate under the ENSEMBLE reference against its win rate under its
OWN reference on the same 598 frontier matches. Those two arms differ in two ways at once, and the outcome
paragraph credits only one of them. The grok reference is grok-reasoning's own answer, so it endorses the new
contestant's answer on about 93% of matches, while the ensemble endorses it far less often. "Judged under my own
reference" and "judged under a reference that happens to agree with me" are therefore the same condition in that
arm, and they are different claims: vendor affinity versus a mechanical composition effect that would apply to
ANY model whose answers coincide with the reference, whoever produced it.
THE STRUCTURE THAT SEPARATES THEM, all of it already on disk. Every match carries four known letters: the new
contestant's answer, the opponent's answer (different by the disagreement filter), the ensemble reference letter
and the grok reference letter.
  STRATUM SAME - the two references give the SAME letter. The two arms' prompts are then byte-identical, so this
  stratum is a pure noise floor: any discordance is the judge's own stochasticity at temperature, and there is
  no room for a self-preference effect at all.
  STRATUM DIFF - the references differ. The whole effect must live here.
  CELLS, per arm: the reference endorses the NEW contestant's answer, the OPPONENT's answer, or NEITHER.
READOUTS. (1) the size of stratum SAME and the discordance rate inside it, reported as the judge's test-retest
noise - a number the programme has never measured and needs for every paired comparison it has made. (2) the
arm difference within stratum DIFF, McNemar. (3) a Kitagawa decomposition of the whole +7.9pp into a COMPOSITION
component - arm A's cell-specific win rates applied to arm B's cell distribution - and a RESIDUAL rate
component, the part not explained by which model the reference happens to endorse. (4) the residual tested by
McNemar pooled over CELL-MATCHED matches only, where both references endorse the same side.
VERDICT RULE, fixed now. If the residual is below 2pp and not significant, the ARENA-13 claim is AMENDED from
"self-preference" to "reference-agreement leakage" - a more general and, for the paper, stronger statement:
a shared reference inflates whichever contestant mirrors it, and vendor identity need not enter. If the residual
is at least 2pp and significant, both mechanisms are real and both are reported with their sizes.
PREDICTION: composition carries most of it; residual 0-3pp; stratum SAME discordance 5-12%.
Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/decomp_outcome.txt; script tools/analysis/decomp_selfpref.py.

## Registered 2026-09-14 (before looking at any result, ZERO calls) — CONSENSUS-FIT: correctness or consensus, quantified
The ARENA-13 mechanism paragraph rests on four rows of a table: gemini is the most accurate model and the least
consensus-aligned. That is an observation, not a measurement, and the thesis wants to state how much of a
model's standing in a reference-based arena is bought by being RIGHT and how much by AGREEING WITH THE FIELD.
TWO FITS. (A) MATCH LEVEL, where the power is. For every judged match with a known reference letter, a logistic
regression of the verdict on two signed contrasts: KEY (+1 if the first model is the key-correct one, -1 if the
second, 0 if the match is not key-decidable) and REF (+1 if the first model's answer matches the reference, -1
if the second's does, 0 if both or neither). Fitted separately on ARENA-13 arm A (1,800 matches, ensemble
reference) and on the x12 MAIN verdicts (the deployed grok reference), so the finding is not an artefact of the
ensemble construction. (B) MODEL LEVEL, for the interpretable coefficient: the 13-model board's BT theta
regressed on standardised key accuracy and standardised ensemble agreement, with partial correlations, a
permutation test on each coefficient and leave-one-model-out stability, since n = 13 is small and must be
reported as such.
READOUTS. (1) the two match-level coefficients with standard errors, and their ratio. (2) judge accuracy split
by whether the key-correct model is also the reference-agreeing model. (3) the model-level standardised
coefficients, R-squared and the leave-one-out sign stability. (4) how much of the gemini rank deficit the fitted
consensus coefficient accounts for.
PREDICTION: the REF coefficient exceeds the KEY coefficient at match level in both fits, and ensemble agreement
keeps a positive partial coefficient at model level after controlling for accuracy.
FALSIFIER, stated now: if REF is not significantly positive once KEY is controlled, the consensus-alignment
mechanism is not supported and the ARENA-13 paragraph must be softened to an association.
Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/consensusfit_outcome.txt; script tools/analysis/consensus_fit.py.

## Registered 2026-09-14 (before any call) — ORACLE: what survives a PERFECT reference?
Every result of the last two weeks converges on the reference, not the judge, as the binding constraint:
JUDGE-2x2 found judge competence irrelevant once the reference is fixed, ARXIASK measured the reference at 0.726
on the questions that discriminate two frontier models against 0.860 on the pool, and ARENA-13 showed even an
ensemble reference carries a bias against the best model. The claim has never been tested at its limit, and it
is cheap to test: give the judge the ANSWER KEY as its reference.
DESIGN. The same 302 pool questions on which arx_0314 and iask_pro differ, the same judge
(grok-4-1-fast-non-reasoning), the same routed anchor rubric, the same v2 mechanics, pairwise DUAL ORDER, 604
calls. The single manipulation is the content of the reference block: the ground-truth letter and option text
in place of the grok-reasoning answer. The wrapper sentence is left byte-identical, "may be wrong" included, so
the judge is not told the reference is now infallible and only the reference CORRECTNESS varies.
WHY IT IS NOT A SANITY CHECK. ARXIASK measured the judge at 0.788 on the subset where the reference happened to
be correct, not at 1.0. An oracle reference over all 302 therefore predicts roughly 0.79, and the gap between
what is observed here and 1.0 is the judge IRREDUCIBLE error - the part of arena error that no reference,
however perfect, can remove. That decomposition is the number the thesis is missing.
REGISTERED. (1) PRIMARY: accuracy against the key on the 302, against the 0.612 the same configuration scored
with the grok reference. (2) ORDER: the judged win rate for arx against the key 0.593, two-sided binomial -
recovering the order means above 0.5 at p < 0.05, which no format has yet managed on these questions. (3)
PAIRED: McNemar against the ARXIASK pairwise verdicts on the same questions. (4) DECOMPOSITION: observed
accuracy against the ARXIASK reference-correct subset (0.788), and the residual against 1.0 reported as the
judge irreducible error, with the share of remaining errors going to the longer answer.
PREDICTIONS: accuracy 0.78-0.88; arx win rate 0.55-0.65; the order recovered at p < 0.05 for the first time in
the programme; irreducible error 12-22%.
IF ACCURACY STAYS AT OR BELOW 0.70 the through-line is wrong as stated: something beyond the reference - length
preference, the judge own priors - survives a perfect reference, and the central claim of the paper must be
rewritten rather than reinforced. That is the outcome worth the 604 calls.
NOT INCLUDED: a pointwise oracle arm (a further 604 calls) is deliberately deferred; it is only worth buying if
the pairwise arm leaves the picture ambiguous, and it needs its own go-ahead.
Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/oracle_outcome.txt; cache oracle.db; script tools/analysis/oracle_ref.py.

    endorses NEW            247   0.939                    411   0.927

    endorses NEITHER        117   0.701                     69   0.536

  and vendor identity need not enter. This is the more general and more useful statement, and it is also the
  more actionable warning: you do not need a judge, a reference and a contestant from the same lab to get the

- **ORACLE OUTCOME (2026-09-14): a PERFECT reference buys 16.4pp and still does not recover the frontier order.
  The through-line survives but has to be stated more carefully: the reference is the larger FIXABLE part of
  the error, not the majority of it.** 301 of 302 discriminating questions, 596 calls, 1 content-filter refusal.
  (1) PRIMARY: accuracy against the key 0.777 with the answer key as the reference, against 0.612 with the
      grok reference. That is 0.003 below the 0.78-0.88 band I predicted - the prediction is met at its lower
      edge, and well clear of the 0.70 line at which the registration said the through-line would be wrong.
  (3) PAIRED on the same 299 questions: 0.612 -> 0.776, +16.4pp, discordant 55:6, McNemar p=5.4e-11.
  THE INTERNAL CHECK that makes the rest interpretable: split by whether the grok reference had been right.
      grok reference was CORRECT (n=217): 0.788 -> 0.797, +0.009 - swapping in the key changes NOTHING
      grok reference was WRONG   (n= 82): 0.146 -> 0.720, +0.573
      The manipulation acts through reference correctness and through nothing else, which is exactly what a
      clean single-variable design should show, and it rules out the reading that the oracle merely made the
      task easier in some general way.
  (4) THE DECOMPOSITION the thesis was missing:
      reference-induced error 0.165 | judge IRREDUCIBLE error 0.223
      So with a perfect reference the judge still gets 22.3% of the discriminating questions wrong, and its own
      error is LARGER than the part the reference contributes. "The reference is the binding constraint" was
      too strong; the accurate statement is that the reference is the larger part of the error that can be
      FIXED by better tooling, and the remainder is the judge itself.
  (2) FAIL, and this is the result worth the money: even with the answer key in hand the judge does NOT recover
      the arx > iask order. Win rate 0.528 against the key's 0.593, binomial p=0.41.
  (5) WHY IT FAILS, and it is not what anyone would guess. Of the 67 remaining errors, 49 are TIES - dual-order
      abstentions, which the accuracy convention counts as wrong. On the 252 verdicts the judge actually
      COMMITS to, accuracy is 0.929. But the abstentions are not random: the key makes arx the winner on 0.694
      of the TIED questions against 0.575 of the decided ones, so dual-order abstention removes precisely the
      evidence that separates the pair, and the arx win rate on the decided subset (0.528) falls short of the
      key's rate on that same subset (0.575). The frontier order fails on WHICH questions get abstained on,
      not on how the committed calls come out. Of the 18 committed errors, 16 (89%) went to the longer answer,
      which is the length preference reappearing exactly where the reference no longer masks it.
  WHAT THIS DOES TO THE PROGRAMME'S CENTRAL CLAIM. ARXIASK concluded that ranking the frontier needs a
  reference stronger than the models being ranked. ORACLE shows that is necessary and NOT sufficient: the
  strongest possible reference lifts accuracy by 16.4pp, and the order still does not come out, because the
  judge abstains selectively and its residual errors are length-biased. The three levers the paper can now
  name, in the order their sizes are measured: reference correctness (16.4pp), the abstention rule (49 of 67
  residual errors), and length preference (89% of the committed ones). Only the first has been the subject of
  the campaign so far.
  EXPLORATORY, post-hoc, zero calls, adjudicates nothing - the tie convention replayed on the same cached calls:
      dual order (TIE on flip)  n=301, 49 ties | accuracy 0.777 | arx win rate 0.528 (p=0.41) | longer 55%
      order 1 only              n=292,  0 ties | accuracy 0.914 | arx win rate 0.575 (p=0.012) | longer 50%
      order 2 only              n=297,  0 ties | accuracy 0.842 | arx win rate 0.465 (p=0.25) | longer 58%
      Order 1 alone recovers the key order (0.575 against the key's 0.593, p=0.012) at an accuracy of 0.914.
      THIS IS NOT A RESULT AND MUST NOT BE QUOTED AS ONE. Order 2 alone, the same calls in the other
      presentation, gives 0.465 and misses. The two orders straddle the truth by about +-5.5pp around 0.52,
      which is a position effect, not skill, and choosing the order that lands on the key after seeing the key
      is exactly the cherry-pick the dual-order convention exists to prevent. ORDER-1 found the opposite
      ranking of the two orders on the full pool (rho 0.986 for order 2 against 0.958 for order 1), which
      confirms that neither order is dependably better. What the replay DOES establish is the size of the
      prize: on discriminating questions, a judge that commits is right about 91% of the time with a good
      reference, and the entire remaining problem is that its two presentations disagree on the 16% of
      questions that carry most of the separating evidence. Position sensitivity, not reference quality and
      not judge competence, is where the next real gain is.
      Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/oracle_ties.txt.
  Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/oracle_outcome.txt; cache oracle.db; script tools/analysis/oracle_ref.py.

## Registered 2026-09-14 (before looking at any result, ZERO calls) — FORMAT-REF: is GRADING less reference-dominated than COMPARING?
CONSENSUS-FIT measured the reference outweighing correctness 2.7 to 1, but it fitted only PAIRWISE verdicts, so
it cannot say whether that dominance belongs to the format, to the judge model, or to the recipe. Every cache
needed to separate them already exists.
FOUR ARMS, the same signed-contrast logistic (verdict on KEY and REF) as CONSENSUS-FIT.
  (a) PAIRWISE grok, R3 sample (stack_v2_promptv2_grok.db) - the format baseline.
  (b) POINTWISE grok with a reference (pointwise_grok.db), the SAME matches as (a), verdict = the higher grade.
      This is the format contrast, paired match for match.
  (c) POINTWISE grok WITHOUT a reference (pointwise_grok_noref.db) - the NEGATIVE CONTROL. The judge never saw
      a reference, so the REF contrast is computed from a letter it had no access to and MUST come out near
      zero. If it does not, the whole CONSENSUS-FIT measurement is confounded by something correlated with the
      reference rather than by the reference, and that finding outranks everything else here.
  (d) PAIRWISE Mistral, the same R3 matches under the same STACK-v2 recipe (stack_v2_promptv2.db) - the judge
      family contrast, the JUDGE-SWAP pair.
READOUTS. (1) KEY and REF coefficients, their ratio and its bootstrap CI in each arm. (2) the PAIRED difference
in ratio between (a) and (b) over the same matches, resampling matches. (3) the REF coefficient in (c) against
zero. (4) (a) against (d).
PREDICTIONS: pointwise ratio strictly below pairwise; the no-reference REF coefficient within +-0.2 of zero;
grok and Mistral within each other's intervals, because RECIPE-GROK showed the recipe, not the model, carries
the behaviour.
FALSIFIER: if pointwise's ratio is equal or higher, the "grade where answers are checkable, compare where they
are not" rule gains no mechanism from this and stays an empirical regularity.
Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/formatref_outcome.txt; script tools/analysis/format_ref.py.

## Registered 2026-09-14 (before any call) — POSITION-DECOMP: how much of ARENA-13 (1) is the slot the model sat in?
ARENA-13 arm A was SINGLE ORDER with the new contestant always presented as Model A, so nothing cancelled the
position effect, and CONSENSUS-FIT found it winning 0.683 of the matches where neither the key nor the reference
favours a side. DECOMP separately measured the judge's test-retest noise at 5.7% on 299 of these very matches -
the ones whose two arms had byte-identical prompts. Reversing the order on the same population therefore yields
position sensitivity cleanly, as flip rate MINUS a noise floor measured on the same questions rather than
inferred from another campaign.
DESIGN. Re-judge the 598 FRONTIER matches of arm A (against gemini, arx, iask, gpt-4o) with the opponent
presented FIRST. Same judge, same ensemble reference, same rubric and mechanics; only the presentation order
changes. 598 calls. The 299 byte-identical matches are a subset of these, so both readouts come from one pass.
Cross-tier pairs are not reversed: they cannot move the top of the board and would double the cost.
REGISTERED. (1) POSITION: the flip rate between the two orders on the 299-match subset, minus DECOMP's 5.7%
test-retest floor measured on exactly those questions, with a bootstrap CI on the difference. (2) DIRECTION: the
new contestant's win rate presented first against presented second, over all 598, paired McNemar. (3) BOARD: the
13-model board recomputed with dual-order TIE-on-flip verdicts for the frontier pairs and the existing
single-order verdicts elsewhere - does the new contestant still place FIRST? (4) AMENDMENT RULE, fixed now: if
its theta falls below gemini's once the frontier matches are order-balanced, the ARENA-13 (1) failure is
attributed to the single-order design, the ledger row is amended a second time, and the standing recommendation
becomes that incremental arena extension MUST be dual order even where the campaign otherwise economises.
PREDICTIONS: flip rate 12-18%, so a position component of 6-12pp; the win rate drops 5-12pp when it is
presented second; the board puts it 2nd.
Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/positiondecomp_outcome.txt; cache arena13.db (arm "reversed");
script tools/analysis/position_decomp.py.

## Registered 2026-09-14 (before any call) — AGGREGATE: the tie rule is the largest untested lever
ORACLE found that with a PERFECT reference the judge is right on 0.929 of the verdicts it commits to, and that
49 of its 67 remaining errors are dual-order TIES which are not randomly placed - the key makes arx the winner
on 0.694 of tied questions against 0.575 of decided ones. Abstention is therefore deleting precisely the
evidence that separates the frontier pair. The programme has never compared the TIE-on-flip rule against any
alternative that is also order-symmetric; ORDER-1 compared it against keeping one order, which is not a rule
anyone could ship because it requires knowing which order to keep.
POPULATION: the 302 arx/iask discriminating questions, under BOTH reference conditions already cached - the
deployed grok reference (arxiask.db) and the oracle reference (oracle.db). Only the questions those runs
returned a TIE on are touched, about 49 in each, because the decided ones are already at 0.93 and re-judging
them would buy nothing.
TWO TIE-BREAKS, both order-symmetric.
  REPLICATE: two further pairwise calls, one in each order, giving four verdicts; majority wins, 2-2 stays TIE.
  GRADE: pointwise grades for both answers (the POINTWISE arm's own prompt and rubric); the higher grade wins,
  equal grades stay TIE. This one is nearly free at deployment scale and is the shippable candidate.
About 49 x 4 x 2 conditions = 400 calls; capped at 600.
REGISTERED. (1) accuracy on the previously-tied questions under each tie-break, against the 0.0 they score now
by convention. (2) accuracy over all 302 with the tie-break applied, against 0.777 (oracle) and 0.612 (grok
reference). (3) ORDER: the arx win rate and its two-sided binomial with the tie-break applied - under the
DEPLOYED reference this is the question the whole frontier line has been failing, and recovering it at p < 0.05
would mean the failure is reference quality plus abstention, both fixable, rather than a ceiling. (4) how many
ties remain, and whether the residual ties still lean toward arx.
PREDICTIONS: on the tied questions both tie-breaks land 0.55-0.75; GRADE beats REPLICATE, because POINTWISE
abstains less by construction and its errors are unbiased (POINTWISE 2x2); overall oracle accuracy rises to
0.85-0.92; the order is recovered under the oracle reference but NOT under the grok reference, whose 0.726
accuracy on these questions is the prior constraint.
IF THE ORDER COMES OUT UNDER THE DEPLOYED REFERENCE, the scheduler gains a tie-break rule and the frontier
result is rewritten as a fixable aggregation defect. That is the outcome worth the calls.
Output experiment_results/x12_crossdomain/aggregate_outcome.txt; cache aggregate.db;
script tools/analysis/aggregate_ties.py.
